content: The katG S315N mutation is included in the Nipro assay but is not covered by Hain version 1 or version 2. There are minor differences in the codon regions analyzed for the wild type among Hain version 1, version 2, and the Nipro assay. Examples of different line probe assay (LPA) strip readouts include: (a) Hain GenoType MTBDRplus version 1 and version 2 (Hain Life Science, Nehren, Germany) (b) Nipro NTM+MDRTB Detection Kit 2 (Nipro, Tokyo, Japan). In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned an updated systematic review to evaluate the accuracy of commercial LPAs for detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid. Among 94 datasets, 83 evaluated Hain version 1, five evaluated Hain version 2, and six evaluated the Nipro assay. Only one study conducted head-to-head testing of all three LPAs on both directly tested clinical specimens and indirectly tested isolates, with these data included as six separate datasets. No studies performed LPA testing on specimens and culture isolates from the same patients, preventing direct within-study comparisons. Following the 2015 review, WHO’s Global TB Programme convened a Guideline Development Group (GDG) in March 2016 to assess the data and update the 2008 policy recommendations on using commercial LPAs to detect MTBC and resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin. LPAs were compared with phenotypic culture-based drug susceptibility testing (DST) as the reference standard, as well as a composite reference standard combining genetic sequencing results with phenotypic DST results. Phenotypic DST was the primary reference standard applied to all participants for all analyses. These analyses were stratified by susceptibility or resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid, or both, and by the type of LPA testing (direct or indirect). Key clinical questions included: 1. Should LPAs guide clinical decisions to use rifampicin in direct testing of specimens and indirect testing of culture isolates in patients with suspected TB? 2. Should LPAs guide clinical decisions to use isoniazid in direct testing of specimens and indirect testing of culture isolates in patients with suspected TB? 3. Should LPAs be used to diagnose multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) in patients with suspected TB? Several studies contributed data on either sensitivity (true positives and false negatives) or specificity (true negatives and false positives), but not both. For these studies, univariate random-effects meta-analyses were performed separately for sensitivity and specificity to optimize data use. Results from univariate analyses were compared with bivariate analyses of studies contributing to both sensitivity and specificity estimates. If fewer than four studies were available or substantial heterogeneity was evident in forest plots, descriptive analyses were performed instead of meta-analyses. Forest plots were visually assessed for heterogeneity, variability in estimates, and prediction region width (wider regions suggest greater heterogeneity). The adoption of LPAs for detecting rifampicin and isoniazid resistance does not eliminate the need for conventional culture and DST capacity. Culture and phenotypic DST remain essential for monitoring treatment responses and detecting additional resistance to second-line agents. The implementation of LPAs should begin in national or central reference laboratories with proven molecular testing capabilities, with potential expansion based on a country’s laboratory strengthening plans, personnel availability, and specimen transport quality. Laboratory infrastructure and equipment must meet biosafety and contamination prevention standards. Facilities require at least three separate rooms for DNA extraction, pre-amplification, and amplification/post-amplification procedures. Access to molecular facilities must be restricted, workflows unidirectional, and cleaning protocols stringent. Laboratory staff must be trained and supervised by experienced personnel, and external quality assessment programs for LPA use should be prioritized. Mechanisms for rapid reporting of LPA results to clinicians must be established to enable early diagnosis and treatment. LPAs are designed to detect TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid in direct testing of processed sputum samples and indirect testing of MTBC culture isolates. However, their performance in other sample types (e.g., tissue, cerebrospinal fluid) has not been adequately evaluated. The availability of second-line agents is critical if resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid, or both is detected. For patients with confirmed MDR-TB or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), second-line LPAs are recommended to detect additional resistance to second-line anti-TB agents. Second-line LPAs (SL-LPAs) offer rapid diagnosis, standardized testing, high throughput potential, and reduced biosafety requirements. They detect mutations associated with resistance to fluoroquinolones (e.g., ofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin) and second-line injectable drugs (SLIDs) (e.g., kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin). SL-LPAs can be performed directly on processed sputum samples or indirectly on DNA isolated from MTBC cultures. The assay procedure includes DNA isolation and amplification, detection of amplification products via reverse hybridization, and visualization using a color reaction. Results can be obtained within a single working day. SL-LPAs detect specific mutations in the gyrA and gyrB genes (associated with fluoroquinolone resistance), the rrs gene and eis promoter region (associated with SLID resistance), and the embB gene (associated with ethambutol resistance). However, the accuracy of SL-LPAs for detecting ethambutol resistance has not been determined. Resistance-conferring mutations detected by SL-LPAs are highly correlated with phenotypic resistance to fluoroquinolones and SLIDs. Positive SL-LPA results can guide infection control precautions and treatment decisions. Research priorities include improving understanding of the correlation between resistance-conferring mutations and patient outcomes, reviewing critical concentrations used in culture-based DST methods, determining the limit of detection for heteroresistance, assessing training and quality assurance needs, and evaluating the impact of early MDR-TB treatment on mortality. Additionally, country-specific cost-effectiveness analyses of LPA use in different settings are needed.
